question: Do four-day work week trials sustain output in knowledge work beyond the first year?

coverage.note: Only 6-month self-report trial and UK 6-month pilot mentioned; no dataset tracking 12+ months post-trial with objective output metrics identified.
Iceland and UK pilot policy status noted; Microsoft Japan and Perpetual Guardian NZ not addressed at all, and no 18-36 month post-trial output data given for any named trial.
No revert/abandonment rate or cited reasons found; only 'almost all continued' claims without denominator or long-term follow-up.
No sector/role-type comparative breakdown found in gathered evidence.
AI adoption and workflow changes mentioned as confounders in 4 Day Week Global trials, but no systematic treatment of staffing/business-cycle confounds.
Novelty/Hawthorne effect raised as a hypothesis/risk (UK pilot commentary) but no evidence of measured decay over time within firms.
Self-report vs. revenue-based distinction noted (Nature piece vs UK pilot revenue data) but no systematic cross-study comparison of output definitions.
No count of methodologically credible controlled studies with 12+ month post-trial data, nor convergence/conflict analysis.

contradictions: The 4 Day Week Global summary (doi.org/10.64628/ab.uxwm4jhhy) claims companies 'recently reported increased revenue,' while the UK 2022 pilot summary (doi.org/10.64628/ab.pnrxqpjq9) states revenues 'stayed largely the same' during the trial - these are drawn from overlapping trial cohorts/timeframes and give differing productivity signals that need reconciliation on which metric, period, and sample is being described.

One source (10.54377/c373-9270) asserts most trial companies sustained productivity long-term via workflow/AI adjustments, while another source (10.64628/ab.pnrxqpjq9) raises an unresolved risk that novelty effects will erode the ~25% productivity boost once the four-day week becomes permanent - these represent conflicting predictions/claims about the same population that current evidence doesn't adjudicate with longitudinal data.

scopeContract.decisionAtStake: Whether an organization (or policymaker) should treat 4-day week pilots as evidence to commit to a PERMANENT policy change, versus treating early positive results as a temporary novelty effect requiring more caution/longer trial periods before scaling.
scopeContract.keyQuestion: Does knowledge-work output (productivity, revenue, or output-per-hour) measured 12+ months after a four-day work week trial remain at or above pre-trial five-day baseline, or does it decay back toward baseline/decline?
assumptions: Scope limited to knowledge work / white-collar office settings (tech, professional services, admin), not manufacturing or shift-based frontline work
"Four-day work week" means reduced hours (e.g., 32 hrs) for same pay, the 100-80-100 model, not compressed hours over 4 days
'Sustain output' means productivity/output per employee stays at or above pre-trial (5-day) baseline, not just self-reported satisfaction
Geography not specified by asker; assume global evidence but weight UK/Iceland/US/Europe pilot data as most available
'Beyond the first year' means longitudinal data at 12+ months post-implementation, distinguishing initial novelty effects from steady-state performance
Currency/cost impacts are secondary to the output question but may be assumed relevant if output claims are cost-adjusted
whatWouldChangeTheAnswer: Discovery of multi-year (2+ year) follow-up data from named trials (e.g., Iceland, UK 4 Day Week pilot, Microsoft Japan, Perpetual Guardian) showing output trend after month 12
Evidence that early productivity gains were driven by measurement/selection artifacts (self-selected enthusiastic firms, self-reported metrics) that would not hold under audited output data
Evidence distinguishing output sustainability by task type (e.g., sustained in creative/autonomous roles but eroded in coordination-heavy or client-facing roles)
Evidence of attrition/reversal rate - i.e., what fraction of trialing firms abandoned the 4-day week after year 1, which would itself be a proxy for failed output sustainability
Presence or absence of confounding changes (e.g., simultaneous AI tool adoption, headcount changes) that could mask the true output effect of the schedule change

hypotheses.hypothesis: Output is durably sustained beyond year one: longitudinal data shows productivity/output holds steady or continues improving after the initial novelty period, with low reversal rates.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Finding credible 2nd/3rd-year follow-up data (not self-report) showing output metrics decline back toward or below pre-trial five-day baseline, OR finding a high (>25%) rate of firms reverting to five-day weeks after year one citing output problems.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Initial gains erode over time (novelty effect): output rises in months 1-12 due to enthusiasm/Hawthorne effect but regresses toward baseline or lower by year two as workload/coordination costs catch up.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Finding independently audited multi-year data (e.g., matched revenue/output-per-employee series) showing output remains flat or improved at 18-24+ months with no regression, across multiple independent trials.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Evidence is too thin/heterogeneous to answer at all: almost no trials have output data beyond 12 months, existing data relies on self-report and non-random samples, so the question is currently unanswerable with confidence.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Finding at least 2-3 independent, methodologically credible trials (control group or matched comparison, objective output metric) with data extending past month 12, giving convergent findings in either direction.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Sustainability is conditional/heterogeneous: output holds up in some sectors/roles (autonomous, deep-work-heavy) but declines in others (client-facing, cross-team coordination-heavy), so there is no single universal answer.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Finding that results are consistent in direction (sustained or declined) across a broad range of industries and role types in year-2+ data, undermining the claim of sector-dependent heterogeneity.

summary: No confirmed claim in this evidence set provides objective, multi-year (12+ month) output or productivity data for knowledge-work four-day-week trials, so the question as posed cannot be answered with confidence from what was found. Given this, H3 ('evidence is too thin to answer') is the only hypothesis the evidence actually supports; H1, H2 and H4 remain untested rather than confirmed or refuted.
answerFirst: The evidence available does not answer whether four-day work week output gains persist beyond year one in knowledge work. What exists is: (a) self-reported, ~6-month trial data showing workers "feel" as productive, (b) UK 2022 pilot data (6 months) showing revenue "stayed largely the same," (c) post-trial policy continuation claims ("almost all" companies kept reduced hours) with no denominator, no output metric, and no 2nd/3rd-year measurement, and (d) Iceland's 2015-2019 trial rolled out nationally but without knowledge-work output tracking beyond adoption. No confirmed claim reports objective, multi-year (12+ month) output data, so H1, H2 and H4 are untested and H3 (evidence too thin to answer) is the only hypothesis actually supported by what was found.

hingeNumber.value: 0 (no confirmed claim reports output/productivity data beyond ~12 months post-trial)
hingeNumber.why: The entire question hinges on the existence of a 12+ month, objective-metric dataset comparing pre- and post-trial output. None exists among the 21 confirmed claims. Every claim about 'continuation' (e.g. claim 2, 3, 17) measures policy retention or self-reported/revenue snapshots taken at or shortly after trial end (6 months in the UK case, claim 18), not output at 18-36 months.
hingeNumber.sensitivity: This is not a number that can move 10-20% - it is a structural absence. If even one methodologically credible controlled study with 18+ month objective output data were found, the answer would shift from 'unanswerable' toward either H1 or H2 depending on direction. Absent that, the answer cannot flip by small evidentiary movement - it can only flip by wholly new data appearing.
hingeNumber.source: Coverage checklist - all eight sub-questions on longitudinal/18-36 month/controlled data are marked partial or unanswered

hypothesisVerdicts.hypothesis: H1: Output is durably sustained beyond year one (low reversal rates, steady/improving output).
hypothesisVerdicts.reasoning: No confirmed claim provides output data (self-report or objective) beyond roughly 6-12 months post-trial-start. Policy-retention claims (2, 3, 6, 17) speak to whether companies KEPT the schedule, not whether OUTPUT was sustained at 18+ months. Revenue data (claim 11) covers only the trial period itself (June-Dec 2022), not a follow-up. No claim reports a reversal rate at all, let alone one above or below 25%, so the kill criterion cannot be evaluated and the supporting criterion (multi-year output data holding steady) is also absent.

hypothesisVerdicts.hypothesis: H2: Initial gains erode over time (novelty effect regresses output toward/below baseline by year two).
hypothesisVerdicts.reasoning: The only evidence bearing on novelty effects is a forward-looking author-stated RISK (claim 19: 'there is a danger that once the novelty has worn off ... they may be less motivated') and general Hawthorne-effect replication-failure caution (claim 13). Neither is an observed measurement of output at 18-24+ months, so this hypothesis is neither confirmed nor killed - its kill criterion (independently audited multi-year data showing output stays flat/improved with no regression) is not met by any confirmed claim, but nor is the hypothesis itself supported by observed decay data.

hypothesisVerdicts.hypothesis: H3: Evidence is too thin/heterogeneous to answer at all - almost no trials have output data beyond 12 months, existing data relies on self-report/non-random samples.
hypothesisVerdicts.reasoning: This is the hypothesis the confirmed evidence actually supports. The coverage checklist explicitly states no dataset tracks 12+ month output with objective measures, no reversion rate exists, no sector breakdown exists, and no controlled study with 12+ month follow-up was found. The kill criterion (2-3 independent methodologically credible trials with control/matched comparison and objective metrics extending past month 12, with convergent findings) was not met - no such trials appear among the 21 confirmed claims. Existing productivity findings are explicitly self-reported (claim 1, audited only 'partial') or single-snapshot revenue figures within the ~6-month trial window (claim 11), consistent with H3's premise.

hypothesisVerdicts.hypothesis: H4: Sustainability is conditional/heterogeneous by sector or role type (autonomous/deep-work vs. client-facing/coordination-heavy).
hypothesisVerdicts.reasoning: No confirmed claim disaggregates output or continuation outcomes by industry sector or role type. The coverage checklist explicitly flags this as unanswered ('No sector/role-type comparative breakdown found in gathered evidence'). Neither the kill criterion (consistent direction across industries) nor supporting evidence (divergent results by sector) is present.

strongestArgumentAgainst: The steelman against 'evidence is too thin to answer' is that the pattern across independent, geographically diverse trials (UK, Ireland, Iceland, 4 Day Week Global's six-country cohort) is strikingly consistent in one direction: policy retention rates are very high ('almost all' companies continuing, 88% full-schedule adoption, Iceland's 86% national rollout), revenue/output did not decline in any snapshot measured, and companies report structural adaptations (workflow redesign, fewer meetings, AI adoption) that are inherently durable, not novelty-dependent. A skeptic could argue that convergent policy-retention data across multiple independent trials, even without formal 18-36 month audited output series, constitutes meaningful real-world revealed-preference evidence: firms with genuine access to reverting to five days largely choose not to, and firms are financially motivated to reverse a costly policy quickly if output truly suffered - the absence of a documented reversal wave is itself informative. However, this counter-argument has a survivorship-bias problem: only companies that succeeded and volunteered continued data likely appear in these follow-up reports (selection bias), the trial designs themselves were opt-in and self-selected toward motivated, resource-rich employers, and 'policy retention' is a poor proxy for 'output sustained' since firms may keep the policy for morale/retention/PR reasons even if output softened moderately - none of the confirmed sources rule this out because none actually measured output at the relevant multi-year horizon.
whatWouldChangeThisCall: A follow-up Nature Human Behaviour or peer-reviewed study measuring the same six-country 4 Day Week Global cohort's objective output/revenue metrics at 18-36 months post-trial.
Disclosure of a reversion/abandonment rate (with reasons) among the ~200 companies and 61 UK organisations that trialed reduced hours, tracked over 2-3 years.

Any credible source reporting Microsoft Japan's or Perpetual Guardian NZ's (flagship trials) output metrics beyond the initial trial period, which are currently entirely absent from this evidence base.
A controlled/matched-comparison study isolating four-day-week effects from concurrent AI-driven productivity tooling adoption, which currently confounds the workflow-adjustment narrative in claim 3.
Sector- or role-type-disaggregated multi-year data that would let H4 (heterogeneous sustainability) be tested rather than remain untested.
baseRate: No outside-view base rate for long-run (2-3 year) productivity persistence in workplace pilot programs is present in the confirmed evidence. Analogous literature on the Hawthorne effect (claim 13) warns that "many studies failed to find the effect at all" and that secondary reporting on novelty/output effects is frequently inaccurate - suggesting caution is warranted, but this is not a quantified base rate for four-day-week output specifically, and the specific "30% of SD decaying to 20% after 9+ weeks" Hawthorne decay figure was explicitly refuted/killed by provenance checks and cannot be used.

findings.claim: Trial-end and early post-trial data (largely self-reported or single-snapshot revenue figures, mostly within 6 months of trial start) show no productivity loss and often perceived productivity gains, but this is not evidence of durability beyond year one.
findings.evidence: Nature news piece: 'workers are happier and feel just as productive' (self-report, claim 1); UK pilot: 'Revenues stayed largely the same' over the June-Dec 2022 trial period (claim 11, 18); 4DWG summary: 'Most companies have been able to implement changes without sacrificing productivity' post-trial (claim 3).
findings.citationCheck: supported for each individual claim, but claim 1's audit was only 'partial' - the fetched page's headline implies self-report but body text does not explicitly confirm the self-report-vs-objective-metric characterization; treat productivity finding as self-reported per headline framing only.

findings.claim: A large majority of trial participants (companies) retained reduced-hours policies after their trials ended, and 88% implemented a full four-day schedule vs. 12% an alternative reduced-time schedule - but 'continuation of policy' is not the same as 'sustained output', and no denominator or churn/reversion rate over multiple years is reported.
findings.evidence: 'almost all of the companies that participated ... have decided to continue with a reduced working hours model' (claim 2); 'Most companies ... continued reduced worktime models after the trial ended' via workflow adjustments, fewer meetings, new tech/AI (claim 3); 88%/12% schedule-type split (claim 12); Iceland rollout to 86% of workforce without pay cut (claim 6); companies 'recently reported increased revenue' with fewer resignations/absences (claim 17).
findings.citationCheck: all individually supported by blind audit, but 'almost all' and '88%' lack a defined long-term (multi-year) time horizon - policy retention is being conflated with output sustainability, which is an inferential leap not licensed by the underlying quotes.

findings.claim: A specific, credible risk was raised in the literature itself: once novelty wears off after the four-day week becomes permanent policy, employees may be less motivated to sustain the ~25% productivity boost needed on working days - directly cutting against durability.
findings.evidence: 'There is a danger that once the novelty has worn off ... they may be less motivated to produce the 25% boost in productivity on the four days they do work' (claim 19).
findings.citationCheck: supported - this is a hedged, forward-looking risk stated by the source author, not an observed outcome; no data confirms or refutes whether this risk has materialized.

findings.claim: Methodological caution is warranted: the Hawthorne-effect literature independently documents that secondary reporting on workplace intervention effects is often factually inaccurate and that many studies fail to replicate claimed productivity effects at all, which bears on how much weight to give short-duration four-day-week trial results.
findings.evidence: 'J. G. Adair warned of gross factual inaccuracy in most secondary publications on the Hawthorne effect and that many studies failed to find it' (claim 13).
findings.citationCheck: supported - this is a general methodological caution from a different literature (workplace psychology), used here as an inference-supporting analogy, not direct evidence about four-day-week trials specifically.

findings.claim: No confirmed claim reports output/productivity metrics at the flagship trials (Iceland, UK 2022 pilot) measured at 18-36 months post-trial, and Microsoft Japan and Perpetual Guardian NZ - commonly cited flagship trials - are entirely absent from the confirmed evidence set.
findings.evidence: Coverage checklist: 'Iceland and UK pilot policy status noted; Microsoft Japan and Perpetual Guardian NZ not addressed at all, and no 18-36 month post-trial output data given for any named trial.'
findings.citationCheck: not applicable - this is an evidence-gap finding, not a sourced claim; flagged as an assumption/gap rather than a fact.

caveats: Several unanswered/partial sub-questions remain: (1) no dataset tracks knowledge-work output 12+ months post-trial using objective (not self-report) measures; (2) no reversion/abandonment rate with cited reasons was found - 'almost all continued' lacks a denominator and time horizon; (3) no sector/role-type (autonomous vs. client-facing) comparative breakdown exists; (4) confounders (AI adoption, staffing changes, business cycle) are mentioned only qualitatively for the 4 Day Week Global trials, not systematically assessed; (5) the novelty/Hawthorne-effect decay hypothesis is raised but never measured within four-day-week firms specifically - and a specific quantified Hawthorne decay figure (30%→20% of SD) was explicitly refuted by provenance checks and must not be relied upon. Many sources carry T? (unknown/unverifiable) tier rather than T1, including the most detailed 4 Day Week Global and UK pilot figures (claims 2,3,7,8,11,12,14,16,17,18,19,20) - none of these achieved T1 sourcing, meaning even 'supported' audits rest on secondary/aggregator-style pages rather than the primary Nature Human Behaviour paper itself. Claim 1's audit was only 'partial' (self-report characterization inferred from headline, not confirmed in body text). Two direct contradictions were flagged and are not resolved: (a) 4 Day Week Global claim of 'increased revenue' vs. UK pilot claim of revenue 'stayed largely the same' - likely different/overlapping cohorts and time windows, not reconciled; (b) claims of sustained productivity via workflow/AI adjustments vs. an unresolved author-raised risk that novelty-driven productivity gains will erode once the policy becomes permanent. Four lower-ranked claims were never verified and are excluded entirely from this report. Two claims (0, 4, 9, 13, 15) come from academic/T2 sources but are either about paper framing/methodology/relevance rather than substantive findings, or (claim 4, 9) concern an unrelated K-12 school-week poll with no bearing on knowledge-work output. This is a fast-moving policy area (UK pilot 2022, Nature Human Behaviour paper 2025) - findings may be superseded by newer multi-year data not yet captured here.
openQuestions: Do any of the named flagship trials (Microsoft Japan, Perpetual Guardian NZ) have documented output data at any post-trial horizon, and why are they absent from this evidence set entirely?
What is the actual reversion/abandonment rate among four-day-week trial participants over a 2-3 year window, and what reasons (output-related or otherwise) do reverting firms cite?

Can the 'almost all companies continued' and '88% full-schedule adoption' figures be reconciled with an objective output metric tracked over the same multi-year period, rather than treated as a proxy for sustained productivity?
Does the novelty-effect risk explicitly raised in claim 19 have any empirical measurement within four-day-week firms specifically, as opposed to being an unverified forward-looking concern?
